geography_and_influence: Punjab’s fertile alluvial plains, rivers and extensive canal irrigation support wheat, rice, mustard and dairy farming. Hot summers and cool winters shape the growing seasons, while the wetter foothills contrast with the drier south-west.
culinary_landscape: Wheat rotis, rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, curd and buttermilk are common everyday foods. Sarson da saag, makki di roti, stuffed parathas and tandoor breads are popular, with local habits varying across the region.

geography_and_influence: West Bengal stretches from Himalayan foothills across fertile river plains to the Ganga delta and coast. Monsoon rain supports rice fields, while rivers, ponds, wetlands and estuaries provide freshwater and brackish-water fish.
culinary_landscape: Rice is usually served with dal, vegetables and fish or meat. Mustard-flavoured fish, posto, street snacks and milk-based sweets are familiar foods; everyday meals and ingredients differ between the hills, western districts and delta.

geography_and_influence: The Kaveri delta, long coastline and dry inland plains create different growing areas. North-east monsoon rain supports delta rice, while millets, pulses, groundnuts and other crops are important in drier districts.
culinary_landscape: Rice meals with sambar, rasam and vegetables are common. Idli, dosa, millet dishes, seafood and meat preparations are also popular; Chettinad, Kongunadu, delta and coastal traditions use different ingredients and spice blends.

geography_and_influence: Kerala’s coast, backwaters and Western Ghats bring heavy monsoon rain and varied growing conditions. Lowlands support rice and coconut, while the hills grow spices such as pepper and cardamom; rivers and coastal waters support fishing.
culinary_landscape: Rice, fish curries and coconut-based dishes are common, alongside puttu, appam, idiyappam and tapioca. Sadya is served for festivals, while Malabar, central Kerala and Travancore have distinct dishes and community food traditions.

geography_and_influence: Rajasthan’s Thar Desert, Aravalli range and semi-arid plains bring low and uneven rainfall. Sandy soils and water scarcity favour hardy crops such as bajra, pulses and gram, while wetter eastern areas support a wider range of crops.
culinary_landscape: Bajra and wheat breads, pulses, dairy, gram-flour dishes and preserved vegetables are common. Dal baati churma, gatte ki sabzi and ker-sangri are familiar foods, with preferences varying between Marwar, Mewar and eastern districts.

geography_and_influence: Gujarat’s dry Kutch and Saurashtra, central plains and long coastline create varied farming and fishing areas. Millets, pulses and groundnuts grow in drier districts, while irrigation supports crops such as wheat, rice and cotton.
culinary_landscape: Rotli, rice, dal or kadhi, vegetables and farsan are common parts of meals. Dhokla, thepla and seasonal dishes such as undhiyu are well known; food preferences differ across Kutch, Saurashtra, central and southern Gujarat.

geography_and_influence: Maharashtra includes the Konkan coast, Western Ghats and the drier Deccan plateau. Heavy coastal monsoon rain supports rice and coconut, while black soils and irrigation inland support crops such as jowar, cotton, pulses and sugarcane.
culinary_landscape: Jowar or bajra bhakri, rice, varan-bhaat, pithla and seasonal vegetables are common. Coastal meals often include fish and coconut, while snacks such as vada pav and regional dishes vary across Konkan, Vidarbha, Marathwada and western Maharashtra.

geography_and_influence: Karnataka ranges from the wet Western Ghats and coast to the drier Deccan plateau. Red and laterite soils, black soils and river valleys support different crops, including rice, ragi, jowar, arecanut, coffee and spices.
culinary_landscape: Rice, ragi mudde, jowar rotti, dosa and idli are everyday staples in different areas. Bisi bele bath, Udupi vegetarian food and coastal seafood are well known; food habits vary between the coast, Malnad, northern and southern districts.

geography_and_influence: The Ganga-Yamuna plains have fertile alluvial soils and support wheat, rice, sugarcane and pulses. The Terai is wetter, while Bundelkhand is drier and more rocky, creating different crops and food supplies across the region.
culinary_landscape: Wheat rotis and rice are common staples, usually served with dal and vegetables. Awadhi kebabs and biryani, Braj sweets, eastern snacks and Bundelkhand dishes add regional variety to everyday home cooking.

geography_and_influence: The Brahmaputra and Barak valleys have fertile river soils, heavy monsoon rain and a humid climate. These conditions support rice fields, ponds and river fishing, while the hills and forests provide bamboo shoots, greens and seasonal produce.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the main staple, often eaten with fish, leafy vegetables and simple dals. Khar and masor tenga are well-known preparations; pork, fermented foods and bamboo shoots feature in some community traditions, which vary across Assam.

geography_and_influence: The Godavari and Krishna deltas, long coast and inland dry plateau create varied growing conditions. Alluvial delta soils support rice, while red soils and lower rainfall inland favour crops such as millets, pulses, groundnuts and chillies.
culinary_landscape: Rice meals with pappu, pulusu, pachadi and pickles are common. Coastal food often includes fish and seafood, while Rayalaseema is known for spicier dishes and greater use of millets and groundnuts.

geography_and_influence: Arunachal Pradesh’s steep Himalayan hills, deep valleys and heavy monsoon rain create many small growing zones. Rice and maize are cultivated where slopes allow, while forests and home gardens provide bamboo shoots, greens, herbs and fruit.
culinary_landscape: Rice and maize are common staples, served with boiled vegetables, leafy greens, bamboo shoots and local herbs. Pork, fish and fermented foods are important in some communities; ingredients and cooking styles differ across tribal groups.

geography_and_influence: The Ganga plain and its tributary floodplains have fertile alluvial soils suited to rice, wheat, maize and pulses. The southern plateau is drier and more uneven, so rainfall and crop choices differ between northern and southern districts.
culinary_landscape: Rice and wheat are everyday staples, with dal, vegetables, sattu and seasonal greens. Litti chokha, fish dishes in river areas and sweets such as khaja are familiar; food preferences vary across Mithila, Bhojpur, Magadh and other regions.

geography_and_influence: The Mahanadi basin, forested hills and plateau areas bring different soils and water conditions. Monsoon rainfall supports rice in the plains, while millets, pulses, tubers and forest produce are important in upland and forest communities.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the main staple, often served with lentils, leafy vegetables and seasonal forest foods. Chila, fara and local rice preparations are familiar; millet dishes and ingredients such as mushrooms and bamboo shoots are important in some communities.

geography_and_influence: Goa’s narrow coastal plain, estuaries and Western Ghats bring heavy monsoon rain and varied soils. Rice grows in low-lying fields, while coconut, cashew and spices grow in suitable areas; the coast and rivers support fishing.
culinary_landscape: Rice, fish curry and coconut-based dishes are common in many households. Xacuti, vindaloo, sorpotel and bebinca are well known, while Hindu and Christian communities maintain distinct food traditions and festive dishes.

geography_and_influence: Haryana’s fertile alluvial plains support wheat, mustard, rice and sugarcane, with drier south-western areas relying more on hardy crops and irrigation. Hot summers, cool winters and uneven rainfall shape the farming calendar.
culinary_landscape: Wheat rotis, bajra, dal, curd, buttermilk and seasonal vegetables are common. Bajra khichdi, kadhi, churma and dairy-based foods are familiar, with meals varying between the irrigated plains and drier districts.

geography_and_influence: Himachal Pradesh’s mountains and valleys change sharply with altitude. Terraced fields and varied soils support maize, wheat, rice, millets, pulses and fruit, while cooler high areas have shorter growing seasons than the lower valleys.
culinary_landscape: Maize and wheat are common grains, with rice, lentils, beans and seasonal vegetables also eaten. Siddu, madra and dishes served during the traditional dham feast are familiar; food differs across Kullu, Kangra, Chamba and other valleys.

geography_and_influence: Jharkhand’s Chota Nagpur plateau, forests and river valleys have red and lateritic soils and a strong monsoon season. Rice grows in suitable lowlands, while millets, pulses, tubers and forest foods support many rural communities.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the main staple, often eaten with leafy vegetables, lentils and seasonal forest produce. Dhuska, chilka roti and rugra mushroom preparations are regional favourites; food traditions vary among Adivasi and other communities.

geography_and_influence: Madhya Pradesh’s plateaus, river valleys and forested highlands have varied black, red and yellow soils. Rainfall and irrigation support wheat, soybean, pulses and rice in different areas, while millets remain important in some regions.
culinary_landscape: Wheat rotis, rice, dal and seasonal vegetables are everyday foods. Poha is popular in Indore, while dal bafla and tribal millet or maize dishes reflect different regional food traditions across the state.

geography_and_influence: Manipur’s central Imphal Valley has fertile fields and wetlands, while hills surround it on all sides. Monsoon rain supports rice cultivation, and rivers, ponds and Loktak Lake provide fish and aquatic plants.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the staple, commonly eaten with fish, vegetables and herbs. Eromba, singju and dishes using fermented fish are familiar; food preferences differ between Meitei communities and the many hill communities.

geography_and_influence: Meghalaya’s Khasi, Jaintia and Garo hills receive heavy rainfall, with cooler highlands and warmer valleys. Hill soils and terraced fields support rice, maize, potatoes and vegetables, while orchards grow fruits such as oranges and pineapples.
culinary_landscape: Rice is a staple, often served with meat, greens and local vegetables. Jadoh, tungrymbai and smoked pork are well known, while food preferences and ingredients differ among Khasi, Jaintia and Garo communities.

geography_and_influence: Mizoram’s steep hills and valleys receive heavy monsoon rain. Shifting and terrace cultivation support rice, maize and vegetables, while forests and home gardens provide bamboo shoots, leafy greens, herbs and seasonal produce.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the main staple, commonly served with boiled vegetables, bai and smoked meat. Pork, bamboo shoots, herbs and fermented ingredients are widely used, though food preferences vary among Mizo communities and households.

geography_and_influence: Nagaland’s mountain ridges, forested slopes and narrow valleys have a humid monsoon climate. Rice and maize grow on hill farms, while forests and gardens provide bamboo shoots, greens and other seasonal ingredients.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the main staple in many Naga communities. Smoked pork, boiled greens, bamboo shoots and fermented foods such as axone are familiar, with ingredients and preparation styles varying among Naga communities.

geography_and_influence: Odisha extends from the Mahanadi delta and coast to the Eastern Ghats and forested interior. Monsoon rain and fertile delta soils support rice, while coastal waters and Chilika lagoon provide fish; uplands grow millets and pulses.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the main staple, commonly paired with dal, vegetables or fish. Dalma, pakhala, temple foods and chhena sweets are well known; millets and forest foods remain important in several upland and tribal communities.

geography_and_influence: Sikkim rises from warm river valleys to cold high mountain areas, so growing conditions change with altitude. Monsoon rain supports rice, maize, ginger and cardamom in suitable areas, while higher villages have shorter growing seasons.
culinary_landscape: Rice, maize, buckwheat and local vegetables are eaten across the state. Momo, thukpa, phagshapa and fermented greens are familiar foods, with Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali communities maintaining distinct traditions.

geography_and_influence: Telangana lies on the Deccan plateau, with red and black soils and hot, often dry conditions. Monsoon rain, tanks and irrigation support rice in some areas, while jowar, pulses, groundnuts and chillies grow across other districts.
culinary_landscape: Rice and jowar are important staples, served with pappu, pulusu, vegetables and pickles. Sarva pindi is a familiar snack, while Hyderabad has a distinct biryani and meat-cooking tradition alongside rural millet-based food.

geography_and_influence: Tripura’s hill ranges and river valleys have warm, humid monsoon conditions. Rice is grown in the valleys, while bamboo, fruit and vegetables grow in hill areas; rivers and ponds provide fish for local meals.
culinary_landscape: Rice is the staple, commonly eaten with fish, vegetables and fermented berma. Mui borok, chakhwi and bamboo-shoot preparations are familiar in Indigenous Tripuri food traditions, alongside Bengali food traditions in the state.

geography_and_influence: Uttarakhand ranges from high Himalayan slopes to the warmer Terai plains. Terraced mountain farms grow millets, pulses and seasonal vegetables, while deeper lowland soils support more rice and wheat; winters are cold at higher elevations.
culinary_landscape: Mandua, jhangora, rice and wheat are eaten in different areas, often with lentils and local greens. Kafuli, chainsoo and phanu are familiar dishes, with Kumaoni, Garhwali and Terai food traditions differing.

geography_and_influence: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands have forested interiors, narrow coasts, mangroves and coral waters. Heavy tropical rain and limited flat land shape cultivation; coconut, rice and tubers are grown, while the surrounding sea provides fish.
culinary_landscape: Rice, fish, seafood, coconut and tubers are common foods, though traditions differ between the island groups. Nicobari foodways include distinctive local ingredients and practices, while migrant communities have brought other regional cuisines.

geography_and_influence: Chandigarh lies on the northern plains near the Shivalik foothills, but urban growth leaves little farmland within the city. Its food supply is closely linked to the surrounding irrigated Punjab and Haryana plains.
culinary_landscape: Wheat breads, rice, dal, dairy foods and North Indian vegetables are common. Punjabi and Haryanvi dishes, tandoori foods, chickpea snacks and street food are widely available, reflecting the city’s mixed urban population.

region_name: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
geography_and_influence: This Union Territory combines inland hills and forests with the coasts of Daman and Diu. Monsoon rain supports rice, millets and tubers inland, while the Arabian Sea and estuaries make fishing important along the coast.
culinary_landscape: Rice, millets, tubers and seasonal greens feature in inland food traditions, while coastal meals include fish and seafood. Daman and Diu also have distinct street-food and Portuguese-influenced traditions; the territory does not have one uniform cuisine.

geography_and_influence: Delhi sits on the Yamuna floodplain beside the rocky Delhi Ridge. Hot summers, winter cold and monsoon rain shape seasonal produce, but most food supplies now arrive through regional farms and wholesale markets beyond the city.
culinary_landscape: Wheat breads, rice, dal and vegetables are everyday foods. Old Delhi is known for chaat, kebabs, biryani and sweets, while Punjabi, Mughlai and many migrant cuisines contribute to the city’s varied food culture.

geography_and_influence: The Kashmir Valley, Jammu plains and Himalayan districts have different soils and climates. Valley orchards and fields support rice, fruit and saffron in selected areas, while warmer Jammu districts grow wheat, maize, rice and pulses.
culinary_landscape: Rice is central in the Kashmir Valley, while wheat and maize are common in parts of Jammu. Wazwan, household curries, kahwa and dried vegetables are familiar in Kashmir; Dogra and other communities have distinct food traditions.

geography_and_influence: Ladakh is a high-altitude cold desert with very little rainfall. Farming is concentrated in irrigated Indus Valley settlements, where a short summer supports barley, wheat, buckwheat, peas, vegetables and apricots.
culinary_landscape: Barley, wheat, buckwheat and local vegetables are important foods. Skyu, khambir bread, thukpa, momos and butter tea are familiar, while food habits vary between villages and Buddhist and Muslim communities.

geography_and_influence: Lakshadweep’s low coral islands have sandy, calcareous soils and little land for farming. Coconut grows widely, but the surrounding reefs and lagoons provide the main food resource; the south-west monsoon brings heavy seasonal rain.
culinary_landscape: Rice is commonly eaten with fish and coconut-based accompaniments. Tuna, dried fish, fish curries and coconut preparations are familiar, while Minicoy has distinct food traditions and cultural links with the Maldives.

geography_and_influence: Puducherry’s four separated enclaves have different coastal and river settings. The Cauvery delta supports rice, while the coast provides fish and coconut; hot weather, monsoon rain and local waterlogging shape farming and fishing seasons.
culinary_landscape: Rice meals, sambar, seafood and local vegetables are common in Puducherry and Karaikal. Mahe shares Kerala food influences, Yanam reflects Telugu traditions, and Puducherry’s bakeries preserve elements of Franco-Tamil food culture.
